explanations.explanation: Elisha, the man chosen to take over from Elijah the prophet (1 Kings 19:16), says, "As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." That's not a maybe. He puts an oath on it. Elijah asked nicely and got a promise back. So they went down to Bethel together.

explanations.answer: He will wait there for Elijah
explanations.explanation: Elijah, the prophet, did ask Elisha to stay here. Elisha didn't take the offer. He answered, "As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." Sitting in the lobby was not on his list, so he went down to Bethel with Elijah.

explanations.answer: He will catch up in a few days
explanations.explanation: There's no catching up later in this story. Elisha, the one picked to follow Elijah the prophet (1 Kings 19:16), says, "I will not leave you." Then the text says, "So they went down to Bethel." Nobody's falling behind on his watch.

explanations.answer: If he knows the LORD will take his master today
explanations.explanation: The sons of the prophets, a group of prophets at Bethel, come out and ask, "Do you know that the LORD will take your master away from you today?" The master is Elijah. They bring up the news, and the news is about today. That's a big thing to hear on a walk.

explanations.answer: If he will stay and lead the prophets there
explanations.explanation: Nobody asks Elisha to lead anything here. The sons of the prophets at Bethel ask him about his master. Their question is, "Do you know that the LORD will take your master away from you today?" Staying put isn't part of their question.

explanations.answer: If Elijah has come to speak to all of them
explanations.explanation: The prophets at Bethel do come out, but they come out to Elisha. They don't ask about a speech from Elijah. They ask, "Do you know that the LORD will take your master away from you today?" It's a question about what's coming, not about a visit.
Not quite. Elisha says, "Yes, I know." So he had already heard it before they asked. Then he adds, "Do not speak of it." I think he's got a lot on his heart right then.
Right. Elisha doesn't act surprised at all. He answers, "Yes, I know," and then says, "Do not speak of it." He already knew, and he was walking on anyway. I think that tells you a lot about him.
Elijah says, "Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me on to the Jordan." Bethel, then Jericho, then the river. Elijah keeps saying it's the LORD sending him. And yes, Elisha keeps walking.

Samaria does show up in this chapter, but at the very end, when Elisha returns there (2 Kings 2:25). At Jericho, Elijah says the LORD has sent him on to the Jordan. That's the next stop. Samaria is a long way down the road.
Bethlehem isn't on this walk at all. The trip goes from Gilgal to Bethel to Jericho. Then Elijah says, "Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me on to the Jordan." The river is the next stop.

Yes. Elisha says the same words a third time: "As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." Three asks, three answers, and the answer never changed. So the two of them went on.
Elisha doesn't give in. He says again, "As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." It's the same oath as before. Then the text says, "So the two of them went on."

Elijah took his cloak, rolled it up, and struck the waters. The river did the rest, because the waters parted. A rolled up cloak is not much of a tool, but that is what he used. Friend, I can't even get the dough to leave my rolling pin.
The cloak never goes flying. Elijah takes it, rolls it up, and strikes the waters with it. He holds on to it the whole time. The river is what opens up.
The cloak stays in Elijah's hands. He rolls it up and strikes the waters. Then the waters part to the right and to the left. Nothing gets laid down on the bank.
The waters part to the right and to the left, and the two of them cross "on dry ground." The riverbed isn't wet at all. That's a good way to cross a river. No wet shoes.
The text says no such thing. It says the waters parted and the two of them crossed over on dry ground. Not a boot got stuck. Dry ground, all the way over.

The ground isn't called holy here. The text just says they crossed over on dry ground. The waters parted to the right and to the left, and the two of them walked across. It's a plain word, and it's the right one.

explanations.answer: A double portion of Elijah's spirit
explanations.explanation: Elisha says, "Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit." Elijah offered him anything, and that's what he asked for. I would've asked for a bigger oven. Elisha asked for something far better.

explanations.answer: A long life in the land of Israel
explanations.explanation: Elisha doesn't ask for a long life. He answers, "Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit." Elijah is about to be taken away, and that's what he asks for.

explanations.answer: A blessing on all the prophets
explanations.explanation: Elisha doesn't ask a blessing for the whole group. His request is about Elijah's spirit: "Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit." It's a personal ask, one man to another.
Elijah says the opposite. He tells Elisha, "You have requested a difficult thing." It was not a small favor. Elijah still gave him a way to receive it.
Elijah says, "You have requested a difficult thing." He doesn't call it easy. But he doesn't shut the door, either. He adds, "Nevertheless, if you see me as I am taken from you, it will be yours."

explanations.answer: He must see Elijah taken from him
explanations.explanation: Elijah says, "if you see me as I am taken from you, it will be yours. But if not, then it will not be so." So Elisha has to be watching. Good thing he wasn't going anywhere.

explanations.answer: He must stay beside the Jordan
explanations.explanation: Elijah doesn't tell him to stay anywhere. The condition is about seeing: "if you see me as I am taken from you, it will be yours." Elisha has been walking right beside Elijah this whole time.

explanations.answer: He must wait there for three days
explanations.explanation: No waiting period is mentioned. Elijah only says, "if you see me as I am taken from you, it will be yours." Three days does come up later, but that's how long the fifty men search (2 Kings 2:17). It's not Elijah's condition.

A chariot of fire with horses of fire appeared and separated the two of them. Elijah and Elisha were walking and talking, and then they weren't together anymore. Then Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind.
The text doesn't say surrounded. It says the chariot and horses of fire "separated the two of them." One of them goes up, and the other stays on the ground.
Lifted is close to what happens, but it isn't the word here. The chariot and horses of fire separated the two of them. Then Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind.

Yes. The text says, "As Elisha watched," he cried out, and then he saw Elijah no more. That matters, because Elijah had said that if Elisha saw him taken, it would be his (2 Kings 2:10). Elisha was watching.
Elisha does watch. The text says, "As Elisha watched, he cried out." He saw Elijah go up, and then he saw Elijah no more.
The text says, "taking hold of his own clothes, he tore them in two." Elisha has just seen Elijah no more. I think this was a heavy moment for him.
His clothes don't go in the river. The text says, "taking hold of his own clothes, he tore them in two." It's the cloak that fell from Elijah that he picks up next.
He doesn't leave his clothes behind. He takes hold of them and tears them in two. Then he picks up the cloak that had fallen from Elijah, and he goes back to the bank of the Jordan.

explanations.answer: Where the LORD the God of Elijah is now
explanations.explanation: Elisha strikes the waters and asks, "Where now is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" Then the waters part to the right and to the left. He asks the question out loud, right there on the bank.

explanations.answer: Whether Elijah will ever come back
explanations.explanation: Elisha doesn't ask about Elijah coming back. His question is, "Where now is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" He asks about the LORD, and the water answers.

explanations.answer: Why Elijah left him all alone
explanations.explanation: That's not what he asks. The text gives his words: "Where now is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" It doesn't say why he asked it. I think it's a real question, and the river answers it.
Yes. When he struck the waters, "they parted to the right and to the left, and Elisha crossed over." It's the same thing that happened for Elijah earlier. Elisha did it alone this time.
The river does part. The text says, "when he had struck the waters, they parted to the right and to the left, and Elisha crossed over." He walked across just like before.

explanations.answer: The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha
explanations.explanation: The sons of the prophets, watching from Jericho, say, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." They saw what happened at the river, and that was their answer. Then they went to meet him.

explanations.answer: Elijah will surely come back to them
explanations.explanation: They don't say Elijah is coming back. They say, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." Their words are about Elisha.

explanations.answer: Elisha should not have taken the cloak
explanations.explanation: No one complains about the cloak. They say, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." Then they go and bow to the ground before him.
Yes. The text says they went to meet him and "bowed down to the ground before him." They watched what happened at the river, and they responded right away.
They do both. They go to meet him, and they bow down to the ground before him. Quite the welcome after a walk by the river.
Elisha answers, "Do not send them." They had offered fifty valiant men to search. He said no the first time they asked.
Elisha doesn't give directions. The prophets suggest the mountains and valleys, and he answers, "Do not send them." He says no to the search.
No timing comes up here. Elisha simply says, "Do not send them." The answer is no, with no wait attached.
The fifty men "searched for three days but did not find Elijah." That's a long time to look. They'd have got better results with a map and a good pair of shoes.
The search is shorter than that. The text says the fifty men searched for three days. They did not find Elijah.
Forty days is a number that shows up elsewhere in the Bible, but not here. The fifty men searched for three days. They did not find Elijah.
They never find him. The text says they "searched for three days but did not find Elijah." Nothing was in the mountains or the valleys.
Right. They searched for three days and did not find Elijah. Elisha had told them not to go, and he said so when they came back.

Elisha says, "Bring me a new bowl, and put some salt in it." Then he goes out to the spring and casts the salt in. It's salt, a simple thing, in a new bowl. And he tells them it's the LORD who has healed the water.
Oil isn't mentioned here. Elisha asks for a new bowl with salt in it. Then he goes out to the spring and casts the salt into it.
No sand in this story. Elisha asks for a new bowl with salt in it. He casts that salt into the spring.
Elisha says, "This is what the LORD says: 'I have healed this water. No longer will it cause death or unfruitfulness.'" The word came from the LORD. Elisha is the one speaking it.
Elisha doesn't take the credit. He says, "This is what the LORD says: 'I have healed this water.'" The healing is the LORD's, and Elisha just delivers the word.
Elijah is already gone by this point. Elisha says, "This is what the LORD says: 'I have healed this water.'" It's the LORD who heals it.
The text says the opposite. "The waters there have been healthy to this day, according to the word spoken by Elisha." The fix lasted.
Right. The text says, "the waters there have been healthy to this day, according to the word spoken by Elisha." Not a bad spring since.

explanations.answer: Calls down a curse in the LORD's name
explanations.explanation: The text says he turned around, looked at them, and "called down a curse on them in the name of the LORD." This is a heavy part of the story. Right after that, two female bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of the boys.

explanations.answer: Keeps walking without saying a word
explanations.explanation: He doesn't keep walking. The text says he turned around and looked at them. Then he called down a curse on them in the name of the LORD. This is a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: Asks the LORD to forgive all of them
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says. Elisha turned around, looked at them, and "called down a curse on them in the name of the LORD." It's a hard thing to read, and it's okay to say so.
